title: Sri Lanka will exit IMF program with debt overhang intact: Economist | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 23 November 2026 00:00
-     - 32

Sri Lanka’s progress on macroeconomic stabilisation under the IMF has not been matched by progress in restoring debt sustainability, a leading economist warned yesterday, leaving the country exposed to costly borrowing once the program ends.

Delivering the Guest of Honour lecture at the Sri Lanka Economic Association (SLEA) annual international conference at the BMICH, Australian National University (ANU) Emeritus Professor of Economics Prof. Prema-chandra Athukorala said: “Sri Lanka’s stabilisation record under the EFF program is encouraging, but the available evidence suggests that the program is likely to end with a substantial debt overhang still weighing on the economy.”

Total national debt declined only marginally, he said, from $ 104 billion in 2023 to $ 92 billion in 2025. The IMF projects it will rise to about $ 94 billion by the end of the Extended Fund Facility (EFF), about 20% above the pre-crisis level of $ 77.5 billion. Foreign debt is projected to reach $ 58.9 billion by 2027, about 13% above pre-crisis levels.

He attributed this to a restructuring that relied on maturity extensions and coupon (interest rate) cuts rather than haircuts, or write-downs, on International Sovereign Bonds (ISBs). Ghana, by contrast, secured a haircut of about 37% from its bondholders in 2024. Sri Lanka’s upfront debt service relief of about $ 3 billion could fall to $ 1.8 billion under the new macro-linked bonds if growth exceeds the IMF baseline, or rise to $ 4.3 billion if it falls short.

“Paradoxically, therefore, stronger-than-anticipated economic growth could itself increase the debt-servicing burden,” he said.

Annual debt service payments (principal and interest) have climbed from $ 2.8 billion in 2023 to $ 4.3 billion in 2024 and $ 5.1 billion in 2025, with the Government accounting for 47% of the 2025 total. The debt service ratio, debt service as a share of exports, rose from 15.9% to 24.9% over the same period. Prof. Athukorala said the ratio had already reached the pre-crisis level as repayment of past due interest (PDI) bonds began in 2025. It would rise further once ISB coupon payments resume after 2027.

Interest payments fell from 79.9% of Government revenue in 2023 to 45.5% in 2025, but remain heavy. Assuming a conservative 5% average interest rate on debt of about $ 92 billion, equivalent to 90% of GDP, annual interest would amount to about 4.5% of GDP, or roughly 40% of revenue. That compares with the IMF’s primary surplus target, the budget balance before interest, of 2.3% of GDP. The Government would therefore need to keep borrowing just to meet interest, he said.

With much of the debt in dollars, a primary surplus alone cannot service it, making reserves critical. The IMF’s reserve adequacy measure covers not only the import bill but also debt servicing and potential capital flight if investor confidence reverses. Prof. Athukorala said the conventional measure, months of import cover, was inadequate for a country managing a large debt stock.

The IMF estimates Sri Lanka needs about $ 12 billion in reserves by 2027 and over $ 13 billion by 2030. In 2025, gross foreign reserves of $ 6.5 billion and net foreign reserves of $ 5.4 billion were only 48% and 43% of that target. He questioned the Central Bank’s practice of adding banks’ net foreign assets to official reserves. He said these assets are privately owned, cannot automatically service sovereign debt and could reflect hidden capital flight.

The IMF still expects Sri Lanka to raise $ 1.5 billion in international bond markets in 2027. As of 7 October, 2026, all three major rating agencies still rated it ‘junk’. ISB spreads narrowed from about 1,900 basis points to 520 basis points by January 2025, but still implied a yield of about 9.9%, against 5.5% to 6.5% for investment-grade emerging-market sovereigns.

“The central concern is that borrowing at such high interest rates would perpetuate the debt overhang, leaving a sword of Damocles hanging over the country’s economic future and risking a trajectory of recurrent debt crises similar to Argentina’s,” he said.

He favoured a back-to-back IMF program that undertakes the structural reforms neglected so far over the ‘home-grown’ approach still advocated by anti-IMF ideologues. He also called for export-led reforms and an overhaul of State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs).

“Stabilisation of the economy and placing it on a self-sustained growth path is not simply a technical exercise in macroeconomic management. Its success ultimately depends on the political economy of reform: on building credibility, securing public support and sustaining the commitment needed to carry reforms through,” he said.

title: Foreign-funded mega  projects lag furthest behind | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 23 November 2026 00:21
-     - 11

Foreign-financed mega projects are spending their allocations more slowly than those funded locally, the Finance Ministry’s Department of Project Management and Monitoring (DPMM) said in its review of the second quarter of 2026.

The 26 projects funded by foreign grants had spent Rs. 2.51 billion, or 7.9%, of their Rs. 31.8 billion allocation for the year by end-June. That was only 21.5% of their first-half target. The 66 projects funded by foreign loans spent Rs. 55.13 billion of Rs. 377.19 billion, or 14.6%, reaching 36.4% of their target.

The 116 projects funded by domestic funds performed best, spending Rs. 38.89 billion of Rs. 220.99 billion, or 17.6%, and 47.6% of their first-half target. Two projects financed by local bank loans spent Rs. 270 million of Rs. 2.43 billion.

Foreign financing problems have largely eased. “At present, all projects except one project for which foreign loan funds were suspended have been restarted,” the DPMM said.

Besides the main causes of delay, 11 projects were held back by changes of scope. Eight suffered from suspended disbursements or rising prices of construction and other materials, six from land acquisition delays, another six from climate and weather changes, and three from poor consultant performance.

To clear bottlenecks, the DPMM holds Integrated Quarterly Progress Review Meetings (IQPRMs) in line Ministries, with officers from other Treasury departments taking part. According to the DPMM’s Annual Performance Report 2025, 51 such meetings were held across 25 Ministries last year.

Issues that cannot be resolved at these meetings go to the Public Investment Monitoring and Evaluation Committee (PIMEC), set up under the Public Financial Management Act to take swift decisions on implementation problems. The PIMEC met 21 times in 2025. The most common problem it dealt with was the release of domestic or foreign funds, affecting 18 projects, followed by coordination among stakeholders in nine.

“The authorities implementing the projects should refer unresolved issues in the projects to the Committee for the purpose of obtaining appropriate solutions,” the DPMM said in its latest review.

It placed responsibility for delivering results on those running the projects. “Secretaries to the Ministries and Project Directors bear a significant responsibility in addressing this situation,” it said.

title: Mega projects spend just 15% of Rs. 632 b allocation by mid-year | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 23 November 2026 00:20
-     - 12

The Finance Ministry says it has spent only Rs. 96.8 billion, or 15.3%, of the total Rs. 632.4 billion mega development projects allocation for 2026 by end-June, and blames slow implementation by line Ministries rather than any shortage of funds (see box: Foreign-funded mega projects lag furthest behind).

The quarterly report by the Department of Project Management and Monitoring (DPMM), submitted to the Cabinet of Ministers recently, covers 210 projects that each cost over Rs. 1 billion. Spending reached just 39.3% of the Rs. 246.2 billion target for the 

first half.

The findings raise questions over the Government’s ability to deliver the 2027 Budget, which President and Finance Minister Anura Kumara Dissanayake presented on 12 November as a shift from stabilisation to transformation. The Budget raises capital spending by 35% to Rs. 2 trillion, or 5.1% of GDP, from 4.1%, prioritising roads, railways, rural connectivity, logistics, and some social spending.

Capital spending has lagged well behind allocations all year. Treasury data show capital expenditure and net lending reached Rs. 276.6 billion in the first half, only 16.1% of the annual estimate of Rs. 1.72 trillion. Lower capital spending, together with a surge in revenue, helped the Budget swing to a surplus of Rs. 9.5 billion, from a deficit of Rs. 405.6 billion a year earlier.

The World Bank said in October that the Government had spent only 16.7% of its 2026 capital Budget and about 8% of the Rs. 500 billion allocated for Cyclone Ditwah reconstruction by mid-year. It attributed the shortfall to weak public investment management rather than a lack of funds. The 2027 Budget carries forward Rs. 260 billion of the cyclone allocation, which Fitch Ratings said went unspent in 2026 because of under-execution.

Analysts have also flagged the risk. “Key risk is execution, not funding,” CT Smith said in its assessment of the Budget.

The DPMM review reaches the same conclusion. “Although there was no delay in the release of funds from the General Treasury, financial utilisation remains low due to project activities not being implemented as expected,” the report said. Bills in hand, meaning payments due for work already done, stood at Rs. 12.5 billion.

The shortfall is starkest in the country’s largest road project. The Central Expressway’s Section 1, funded by China, was allocated Rs. 64.15 billion for 2026 but had spent only Rs. 2.88 billion by June, about 4.5%. Section 1 began in September 2020 and was due for completion in September 2024. It is now 50.5% complete, and its deadline has been pushed back four years to September 2028.

Section 3, funded locally, has spent Rs. 7.28 billion of its Rs. 30.5 billion allocation. It started in January 2016 and was due to finish in June 2024, but is 36.8% complete and now has a 2029 deadline. Together, the two sections account for about 15% of the total mega project allocation for the year.

At Ministry level, the Housing, Construction and Water Supply Ministry spent Rs. 9.53 billion against a 1H target of Rs. 48.93 billion, or under 20%. The Transport, Highways, Ports and Civil Aviation Ministry, which has the largest target, spent Rs. 33.66 billion of Rs. 83.58 billion. The Finance Ministry’s own projects performed best, spending Rs. 9.03 billion of a Rs. 10.87 billion target.

Of 47 projects scheduled for completion by end-June, only 10 had been finished. 20 projects made no physical progress during the quarter, and 62 were less than 40% complete.

The review also exposes weak discipline over deadlines. It found that 35 projects were still being implemented after their approved periods had expired, without obtaining formal extensions of time. Another 121 were running on formal extensions, and only 54 were within their agreed time frames. The report said the delays had pushed up costs and changed project scopes, hurting cost effectiveness and holding back benefits to the public.

“Overall project performance has not shown significant improvement, and a large number of projects are being implemented with extension of time,” it said, noting that this was despite earlier problems such as fund release difficulties and suspended foreign loans having eased.

The DPMM’s colour-coding system classified 32 projects as critical because of several time extensions, cost overruns, or other issues. A further 39 need special attention and 70 need interventions to deliver expected results. Only 58 were rated as progressing successfully or properly.

Several long-delayed projects stand out. Construction of the Pallekele Prison Complex began in January 2007 and was due to finish in December 2011. With 203 months of extensions, it is 79% complete and now has a December 2028 deadline. The Defence Headquarters Complex Phase 1, estimated at Rs. 65.45 billion, began in 2011 and was due in October 2016. It is 99.5% complete after 123 months of extensions and is rated critical.

The Indian-funded 10,000 Housing Program had reached only 10.32% physical progress against a target of 45%. It has spent Rs. 356.6 million of its Rs. 4.29 billion allocation for the year.

Of the 39 ongoing projects that are over 90% complete, 12 began before 2016, although they were originally meant to take three to six years. The report urged Ministry Secretaries to finish them without further delay. “This will create financial space for new public investments in accordance with the Government’s policies,” it said.

Contractor performance was the most common cause of delay, affecting 28 projects. It was followed by procurement delays in 22 projects, delays in third-party approvals in 20, and shortages of project management staff in 12. The report also cited short-term fuel supply restrictions, higher fuel prices, and difficulties in obtaining bitumen.

The DPMM also warned that weak exit strategies had left some completed projects without proper operations, staffing, or asset transfers. It said ‘the underutilisation or abandonment of such assets can be observed’ and that it would issue a circular requiring Ministry Secretaries to plan for project completion, handover, and sustainability.

During pre-Budget discussions, the President directed officials to improve the implementation of infrastructure programs. At the agriculture sector review, officials noted that delays in completing projects started in previous years had imposed a significant financial cost on the Government, and it was decided that projects that had missed implementation timelines would be reviewed.

The total estimated cost of the 210 projects is Rs. 3.7 trillion, and a further Rs. 1.8 trillion is needed to complete them.
